meta.title: Who really said "I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it's genuinely William Ernest Henley, the closing couplet of his 1875 poem "Invictus" (first published 1888). Often mis-credited to Nelson Mandela.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely William Ernest Henley — the last lines of "Invictus" (1875, published 1888). Often mistaken for Nelson Mandela, who loved the poem.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: These are the closing two lines of Henley’s poem “Invictus,” written in 1875 and first published in his 1888 collection “A Book of Verses.” The original text reads with a colon — “I am the master of my fate: / I am the captain of my soul” — where the popular quotation usually substitutes a comma.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
It matters not how strait the gate,
How charged with punishments the scroll,
I am the master of my fate:
I am the captain of my soul.
trail: The poem was written in 1875 and first appeared in Henley’s 1888 collection “A Book of Verses”; the now-famous title “Invictus” was attached later by Arthur Quiller-Couch in The Oxford Book of English Verse.
The primary text confirms the closing couplet verbatim — “I am the master of my fate: / I am the captain of my soul” — with a colon where the popular version uses a comma.
The line is often mis-credited to Nelson Mandela, who recited the poem during his imprisonment; Wikipedia documents both the true authorship and the Mandela association.
source.excerptNote: The final stanza of “Invictus.” Note the original colon after “fate” — popular quotations usually replace it with a comma.

sourceLink.text: Read the full poem on Wikisource

source.rightsNote: “Invictus” was first published in 1888 and its author, William Ernest Henley, died in 1903, so both the work and any rights in it are long expired — it is firmly in the public domain worldwide.

author.name: William Ernest Henley
author.heading: About William Ernest Henley
author.bio: William Ernest Henley was an English poet, literary editor and critic who lost a leg to tuberculosis of the bone as a young man and spent long stretches in hospital. He wrote “Invictus” in 1875 while recovering from surgery at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh; its defiant self-mastery grew directly out of that ordeal. Robust and bearded, he was also the model for his friend Robert Louis Stevenson’s Long John Silver.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The words are genuinely Henley’s, but two things frequently go wrong when the line is quoted.

items.why: Because Mandela treasured “Invictus” and recited it during his 27 years of imprisonment — and because of the 2009 film named after it — the lines are sometimes credited to him. Mandela loved the poem; he did not write it. The Academy of American Poets traces the connection.
The popular quotation joins the two lines with a comma, but Henley’s original ends the third line with a colon: “I am the master of my fate: / I am the captain of my soul.”

misattribution.truthLine: The lines are the authentic close of William Ernest Henley’s “Invictus” (1875, first published 1888) — verified against the primary text.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Henley composed “Invictus” from a hospital bed. As a young man he lost his left leg below the knee to tuberculosis of the bone, and later fought to save the other. The poem’s unbowed defiance — “My head is bloody, but unbowed” — is the voice of a man refusing to be broken by his body.

The closing couplet became one of the most-quoted expressions of self-determination in English. It surfaces everywhere from sports locker rooms to the film that shares its Latin title, and it carried Nelson Mandela through nearly two decades on Robben Island.
